utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Any indispensable issues to raise before we start?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just the witness has some protective measures, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And it is Witness Q. We agree? Okay. Then the witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And the witness does have image distortion. That is prepared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only image. Could we have the first break, then, quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, in the meantime, the Defence is prepared to discuss the issue of signatures tomorrow, as planned?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. We have scheduled an appointment to meet with our client tomorrow at approximately 10.00, and me and my learned friend are going to exchange hopefully this afternoon the exact statements in which there might be a dispute. Then tomorrow afternoon, we will be able to advise the Court of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you then, please, give the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. And first of all, my apologies -- first of all, my apologies. You are a protected witness, and therefore, we will not call you as your name, but only "Witness Q." It's not very polite, but it is for your protection. Please understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the examination-in-chief may start, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, could you please move the ELMO to the side, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to show you a piece of paper which has your name on it. Can you please confirm that that is your name without saying your name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If this piece of paper can be shown to the Defence, before the witness, and the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is indeed my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session to ask the witness some background information, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be, just for clarification, Exhibit S118.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And obviously that would you be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence and under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. And private session enough, or closed session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Private session is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No objection. Then please, private session. [Private session].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And we may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Madam, we have just moved into open session, so please try to remember not to mention anything that would reveal your identity. And if that is required, then we can go into private session before you do that. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the day of the takeover of Prijedor by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you go to Prijedor on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I saw the military around the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were they stationed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: All over the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints set up in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: At the entrance to Prijedor, and also all over the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your husband lose his job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: On the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know of other non-Serbs who lost their employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many people do you know that lost their jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: All those who worked in Prijedor who were Muslims, all of them lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: All the people that you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you remember an attack, a shelling, on Hambarine in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to the evening prior to the shelling. What happened that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Five shells fell near where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were any buildings damaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which buildings were these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Mostly the mosque and the surroundings of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you hear on Radio Prijedor in relation to these five shells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We were told to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you told what would happen if you didn't surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you hear on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They said they would keep on shelling us, that we had time until noon the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened at noon the following day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The shelling began again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did the shelling last for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The worst of the shelling lasted for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: During that two-hour period, was the shelling continuous or intermittent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It was continuous.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know from what direction the shelling was coming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What direction was it coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: From the Topic Brdo and from the Prijedor airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know in what part of Prijedor the airport is located, the name of the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you come to know what direction the shelling was coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: My husband was outside, and he knew everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where did you go when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We were in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many of you were in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were many of us, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We stayed for two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We went to the woods, the Kurevo woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As you left the house, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We saw tanks and soldiers passing by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many tanks were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I, myself, saw three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many men did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were quite many soldiers. I didn't count them exactly, but there were lots of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were these soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They were wearing multicoloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of arms did they have, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you saw them, as you left the house heading towards the woods, what were the soldiers doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They were shooting after us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see what the tanks were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what the tanks -- what was happening with the tanks at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They were firing at the houses. They were destroying the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were they destroying the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They shelled houses from the tanks, just destroying them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see any houses burning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As you fled towards the woods, did you see anyone wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, there was one young man who was with me. He was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, not any of the people who were with me, only this young man was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Other than the people who were with you, did you see anybody else that had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I only saw a dead woman as I set out for the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know this lady?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: She was lying across the threshold, and her head was falling down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say: "Her head was falling down," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Half her body was in the house and half was lying outside, and her head was severed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As you ran towards the woods, did you see anybody else in a similar situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw a woman who had been killed. She was lying like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just describe how she was lying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: She was lying face down on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you see, in relation to her body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I saw blood all around her.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session to look at two diagrams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you also want to ask the name?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Madam, we have now moved back into open session. How long did it take you to arrive in the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: About an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was there in the woods when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, one to two hours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the tanks follow you to the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, one of the tanks followed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were they able to enter the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, they were not. They tried to fell trees with chainsaws so that they could get in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "they," who are you referring to, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the tanks stay by the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, one of the tanks remained in the vicinity of the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did it do, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It opened fire in the direction of the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We stayed the whole night and the following day, the whole of the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We went to Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Ljubija for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We stayed quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was happening in Ljubija at this time, during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Serb soldiers came and took people away from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the persons that were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I remember a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you or your husband return to your house during the time that you were in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, he did. My husband came to the house, but he would actually remain in the vicinity of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did he tell you he saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: That he had seen a tank (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to your house, did your husband tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that it was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you remember an attack, a shelling, of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: You mean the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, the month, if you can't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It was in the month of May, but I cannot recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to a time period in Ljubija in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Yes, it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution need a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall any shelling occurring in Ljubija in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I can't remember any of that. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall one day when your husband was taken away from Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Not the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the day, though, even though you don't recall the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but I do remember the day, what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court what happened the day your husband was taken away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In the morning, at 4.00, we were in the cellar. There were women and children, men, too. Then the soldiers came. They banged on our door and told us to get out. Look at this nest of Green Berets, they said. They chased us out. They separated the men from the women and children immediately and took them one by one to the stadium in Ljubija. Other four soldiers came, to separate the women from the children. One of the soldiers said: "Women to one side, and children to the other. We'll make a small Jasenovac out of this place." We started crying, and women started pressing their children against them. A commander came. He was talking to someone using a radio set, and he said not to separate the women from the children. They went into the cellar. They had bayonets, and they started piercing the hay that was piled where we used to lie. They took the men away. They took them away one by one. They took everyone. Then they returned us to the cellar, bolted the door so we couldn't watch. Personally, I could see from the cellar window as they were taking away men with bloodstained heads and their hands tied behind their backs. They were taking them down that road. In the town of Ljubija, there was shooting. There were cries that the town was being shelled. This lasted until after 4.00 in the afternoon, practically the whole day. Just before nightfall, the shelling calmed down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your husband return home at any point, or return to the house where you were staying in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, my husband returned that afternoon from the stadium. He came home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your husband tell you what happened at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: He told me that they were killing people at the stadium, loading them into the vans and taking them to the camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether anyone had been killed at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: He said that many men had been killed at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When the men had been taken away to the stadium, what happened to the women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We were taken back to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the soldiers mistreat you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, they abused us verbally. They kept asking for money. They took away our jewellery.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were these soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were many soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Out of the group of men that were staying in the house with you, how many of the men returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: All but one returned. That one was taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution, could I request a redaction, please, at 15.45.43. The witness referred to a location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Will the redaction please be prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Serb soldiers return to Ljubija that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did they do when they returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Robbing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you leave Ljubija at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I left Ljubija, but only later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: To Gomjenica, to Zeger.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you went to Gomjenica, were you visited by anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Stakic and Kojo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where did Stakic work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: At the Celpak company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: He was not very tall, rather short actually, neither fat nor thin. He had a greying hair, parted on the side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned another person called Kojo. Did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know his name. I just knew him by his nickname. Everybody called him Kojo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know Stakic's first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long had you known these two men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: My husband knew them. I didn't know them very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened when they arrived at the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: When they arrived at the house, he told me husband that he should not move around the fields too much, that he should stay inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "he," who are you referring to, Stakic or Kojo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They both said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was Stakic's occupation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: He was a foreman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did your husband do after they had had this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The next day, he fled to the woods with a friend of his.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did either of these men return to the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: You mean my husband or...?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I mean Stakic or Kojo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, they both returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what did they say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: A neighbour of mine was at the house, the wife of the man who had fled with my husband. And Stakic said that I was would be his wife, and that this other woman would be Kojo's wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move on to another topic. Perhaps this might be an appropriate time to break, or I can for ten minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we proceed, in the absence of the witness, the Bench believes that some remarks are necessary. When there is examination, and we are well aware that we are in an adversarial system, and it's for the party to make the contributions, but it has to be done in a way that the Judges can understand what the contribution shall be. And there are two possibilities, of course: Either the Judges intervene themselves, what we don't want in principle. But as uti moratio, we have to do this. On the other hand, it, from our point of view, it is unfair, an unfair proceeding, to touch, for example, upon a name, Stakic, and then leave it open what person this is, to touch upon, say, as it was -- as you can read it on the transcript, that the two person asked evidently the witness and another female person to be wife, and without going on what happened. So we can't depart. Therefore, this way of examination, only touching upon issues, can't be tolerated. And therefore, I would ask the parties -- we would ask the parties to be more concrete and go into the details and not leave the most important issues open for guessing games for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make a few points. The Prosecution takes on board everything that Your Honours have said, and we agree with what you have said. We discussed this in the break, the fact that we think this witness is very, very nervous, and I was going to speak with her as soon as she came back to the witness box to just ask her to relax a little, that you want to hear the story. And in relation to the second matter about the two names of the witnesses, I saw the last question that I asked, and it was left very open, and I was going to go back to that and close that before I move to the next topic. Your Honour, I also have some very good news for Your Honours, and that is we have our first agreed fact in this case, and this is that the Stakic which the witness has been referring to is not the accused Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As I said earlier, it would have been the adequate time to come -- to let the witness come to this conclusion and hear the evidence in toto, and of course, I'm aware that the witness is especially nervous. But couldn't it be a solution, just let the witness speak in a context, and not always to interrupt. It's extremely difficult for me, as a judge coming from a civil-law system, and please, both parties understand this, normally the protection of the witness and the testimony in context would be the first and foremost work of the Judges. But we have to accept here it's for the parties. But please, then, give room for the parties and let them speak if they so want. And I have the impression this witness wants to tell the Bench the story, and we want to hear it and in a context. So I would like to proceed in this spirit. And the witness may be brought in again. Please be seated again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Madam, you seem to be very, very nervous at the moment. I would ask you to relax as much as you possibly can. The Judges want to hear what you have to say in your own words. We obviously weren't there in 1992, and the Judges need to hear what you have to say in your own context. So please feel free to expand on your answers as we go through your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, I'm a bit nervous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You shouldn't be nervous. You should know that the purpose of our work, and we are mandated to find the truth and to hear what the persons in the country, in former Yugoslavia, have experienced. And it's only you, the witnesses, who can tell us what has happened. And I think it could, and can be, of course, also helpful for you if you can tell us what you have experienced in a context. And therefore, please feel free, if you want, to tell us something, if you want to give us a message, do so. We are here in a private session -- in open session, but we have protective measures, and thereby your personal data is protected, and you can speak to us in a free way and tell us what you want to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult sometimes to tell about one's own experience, especially if it has left traces on one's body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are all aware of this, and please believe us. We are all experienced in this field, and we know about these difficulties, and we know about the difficulties also a witness has in this very special situation. And we understand that it's difficult for you to be here today. But nevertheless, please try to tell us your experiences.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Madam, just before the break, we were discussing when a couple of men came to your house and spoke with you and your husband, at which point your husband left the house, and then these two men returned. You had said a conversation that you had with these two men. Can you please just tell us again what these men said to you and what you responded to them before they left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Stakic told me that I would be his wife, and he told my friend that she would be Kojo's wife. He said: "You will be our wives."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did you respond?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I said: "Shame on you. You want me to be your woman."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They left. My husband came back in the evening, at 2.00 actually. He took a bath, and he wanted to take some food with him to the woods. At 4.00 in the morning, four soldiers appeared -- I'm sorry, no. That's not how it happened. I apologise. Something else happened before. My husband was at home. He arrived at about 2.00. At about 3.00 or 3.30, I heard some noise outside. I peeked through the window, and I saw a group of soldiers pushing a group of people in front of them towards the Zeger bridge. And I told my husband: "You better leave the house. Something is very wrong. They are taking men and women to the Zeger bridge." And he said: "I do not want to leave you. I don't want to flee." I went back to the window, and I realised that they were rounding up many people from the surrounding houses and taking them down the nearby roads. Again, I told him to flee. He didn't want. And at 4.00 a.m., four soldiers with weapons and with masks over their faces came to the house. They banged on the door, and then they broke in. They immediately started beating him in front of me and the children. Me and my children, we started to scream. They took him Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 3938 to 3946. outside. They told him to put on his shoes and get out. They continued beating him in front of me. Those people were not local Serbs. They were Serbs from Serbia, because our local Serbs do not use the word "Bre," and also judging from the way they cursed my husband, you could conclude that they were from Serbia. I told them to stop beating him. I said: "He hasn't done anything wrong." But they continued hitting him. They tied his hands behind his back with a piece of wire, and they told us to go back into the house. I stayed at the window, and I watched him being taken away by these people. They all -- they were hitting him all that time. And at one point, he turned around and he said: "Take care of the children. I'm no more." They took him in the direction of the bridge, and I just watched him being taken away. They put him on to a bus which was there, and that was the last time I saw him. At that moment, I went back into the house. My children were screaming and crying, and this friend of mine whose husband had come back from the woods was also there. Her husband was also taken away. They took everybody away. She came to my house, and I watched through the window what was going on at the Zeger bridge. They brought many people to the bridge. They turned on some music. They had a stereo which they had taken from a nearby house, and they played it very loud, and they started killing people and throwing their bodies into the Sana River. I saw this with my own eyes. I saw them beat up a young man who was covered in blood, and then told to go into the Sana River to wash himself. He bent down to get some water to wash himself, but at that point, they opened fire and shot him at his back, and he fell down into the water. They took a very old man from a nearby house with his son. His son has never come back to this date. And this old man was severely beaten up at the bridge, but he returned. He was black and blue when he returned. And they went on doing this for a while, rounding up many people at the bridge, some of whom never returned. They also forced men to jump down from the bridge, and then they would open fire at them. And their bodies would float on the river. The Sana was red with blood. I could hear them scream and shout. I heard them shouting things such as: "Kill him, cut his throat" but not all of them were killed. Some men were loaded on to the buses and then taken to the camps, to Omarska and Keraterm. Buses were coming and going. They would come back empty. And those who were still alive were then put on these empty buses and taken to the camps. Those who were killed on the spot, their bodies were then thrown into Sana. And throughout that time, the music was playing loud, and the people were screaming.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to go back and clarify a number of things that you have just told us about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said earlier that you looked out of the window and you recognise -- and you saw some people. Did you recognise anyone at that point, the first time when you looked out of the window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised Mico, whose family name now escapes me. He used to drive a local bus at Hambarine. I'm sorry, I cannot remember his family name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Jurusic, Mico Jurusic. I couldn't remember it for a moment. There were quite a few soldiers there. The whole bridge was teeming with soldiers. Some were engaged in killing, and some were engaged in putting people on to the buses. But there were many of them in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the ethnicity of the victims that you have just told us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Those who were being killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, the victims -- yes, sorry. The victims, those that were being killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you recognise any of the people that were initially taken to the bus along with your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go into private session, please, so that the witness can tell us those that she recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Go into private session, and the witness may know that when there is such a question, don't hesitate once again to answer in the context. And nobody can hear now in the outside what will be said and therefore, it may be easier for you to make your statement. Thank you.
